clue.text: Rodent finds some potato by the noise of the frier

parts.note: a chip is a piece of potato

indicators.note: the noise of a word is how it sounds when spoken, so the spelling follows the sound

parts.note: frier is an old spelling of friar, a member of a religious order like a monk, and puns on a chip frier

explanation.surface: A small animal is lured by the sizzling sounds of a chip fryer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the noise of' says MONK is wanted only for its sound, spelt MUNK. 'Frier' looks like the chip pan, keeping up the potato theme, but it is the friar, a monk.
explanation.definitionFit: The chipmunk is a small striped North American squirrel, so it is a rodent.

clue.text: A holiday-maker may be more affected

definitions.meaning: camp means theatrical or exaggerated, so this is the comparative

explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' only links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A tent-dweller on vacation is one sense; the other is the comparative of camp, meaning showily theatrical.

clue.text: Simplicity once uncommon in fashionable northern church

indicators.note: in places the scrambled letters inside the run of fashionable, northern and church

parts.note: in means fashionable
CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: uncommon means unusual, so the letters of the word once are put in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Plainness was once rare in a stylish church in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncommon' scrambles the word once, and 'in' sets the result between the northern abbreviation and the church.
explanation.definitionFit: Innocence is guilelessness, the artless simplicity of someone without worldly experience.

clue.text: John Willet's inn, a centre for dancing

definitions.meaning: in Dickens's Barnaby Rudge, John Willet keeps an inn of this name
a tall pole round which villagers dance on May Day

explanation.walkthrough: John Willet is the landlord in Dickens's novel Barnaby Rudge; his inn is named after the May Day pole.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens named Willet's tavern after the beribboned pole at the heart of traditional spring dances.

clue.text: "The _____ of nations! there she stands" (Byron)

parts.note: a line from Childe Harold about Rome, likened to the Greek mother who weeps for all her slain children

explanation.walkthrough: Byron calls ruined Rome, mourning her lost glory, by the name of the mythical mother turned to weeping stone.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this mother lost all her children to Apollo and Artemis and wept forever, so Byron uses her for grieving Rome.

clue.text: Herb is abnormally shy, so quiet

indicators.note: abnormally says the letters of the following words are arranged in an unusual way

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet

explanation.surface: A plant is described as unusually bashful and silent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abnormally' rearranges SHY and SO to give HYSSO; P, the musical sign for soft, ends it. 'is' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyssop is an aromatic plant of the mint family used in cooking and medicine, a kind of herb.

clue.text: Language of attractive woman after do-it-yourself upset

indicators.note: after places the woman following the other piece
upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the abbreviation is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a dish is slang for an attractive person

explanation.surface: A tongue spoken by a pretty woman after a home-improvement disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns the home-improvement abbreviation upside down, and 'after' puts the woman behind it. 'of' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Yiddish is the Germanic tongue of Ashkenazi Jews, written in Hebrew script.

clue.text: Jeer like Bunter?

definitions.meaning: Billy Bunter, the greedy schoolboy of British comic stories, gobbles food

explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is a fat, greedy schoolboy in Frank Richards's British school stories, always eating.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to mock and, informally, to eat greedily, as the gluttonous schoolboy does.

clue.text: Rule out copyright in one form of music

indicators.note: in puts the copyright symbol inside the musical piece

parts.note: a prelude is an introductory musical piece
C is the copyright symbol

explanation.surface: A ruling bans copyrighted material in a particular musical genre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' slips the copyright sign into the musical piece, three letters along.
explanation.definitionFit: To preclude something is to prevent it from happening, to exclude it in advance.

clue.text: Bank on the Spanish for bad verse!

parts.note: the Dogger Bank is a large sandbank in the North Sea
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Counting on Spanish speakers to produce poor poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank on' reads as 'rely on', but the Bank is Dogger Bank, a North Sea shoal named in British shipping forecasts. 'on' and 'for' only link.
explanation.definitionFit: Doggerel is crude, comic or badly made poetry.

clue.text: Payment in respect of former painter? An easy gain

definitions.text: Payment in respect of former painter?
definitions.meaning: a painter is the rope tying up a boat, so an old painter is an old rope, and payment for it is cash for that
profit earned for little or no effort

explanation.walkthrough: 'Painter' suggests an artist, but on a boat a painter is the mooring line, so a former painter is old rope.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes cash got for something worthless or for no real work, which is an effortless profit.

clue.text: Bound to upset student, one CSE!

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and scrambled, so the following letters are rearranged

parts.note: L, the learner plate, stands for a student

explanation.surface: An exam candidate with a single CSE pass is destined to be disappointed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' reads as 'certain to', but 'Bound' is the definition, a verb. 'upset' rearranges L, ONE and CSE. The CSE was an old British school-leaving exam.
explanation.definitionFit: To bound an area is to mark its limits, or to fence it in on all sides.

clue.text: Lucrative as gallium with no reduction? Not quite

parts.note: Ga is the chemical symbol for gallium

indicators.note: not quite says the phrase stops just short of its end, losing its last letter

parts.note: paid in full means paid with nothing knocked off

explanation.surface: A chemistry question about whether gallium is profitable when undiminished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite' docks the final letter of the phrase 'in full'. 'as' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Gainful work brings in money, so it is profitable.

clue.text: Sophisticated rite for counterfeiting gold up country

parts.note: in can mean fashionable or in the know, a sophisticated thing

indicators.note: counterfeiting is faking, so the letters of the word rite are made into a false form

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: Somewhere inland, a refined ritual for forging gold is performed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'counterfeiting' scrambles the word rite, set between the other two pieces. 'up country' is the definition, the inland part of a land; 'for' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Going up country means heading inland, away from the coast into the heart of a land.

clue.text: Tell-tale attending lessons with hesitation

parts.note: in means present or attending
a form is a school class, where lessons are held
er is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A sneak at school stammers while sitting in class.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools a class is a form. 'with' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: An informer passes on secrets about others to authorities, as a sneak does.

clue.text: Made for a little house by the sea

parts.note: ho is the short form of house
the Med is short for the Mediterranean Sea

explanation.surface: Something was built for a small cottage on the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made for' reads as 'built for', but it means 'headed towards'. 'a little' signals the shortened form HO, and 'by' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A pigeon homed when it flew straight back, so homed means headed for a target.

clue.text: Employee has stock to move without mechanical aid

parts.note: a man is a worker or employee
a shop that handles goods stocks and sells them

explanation.surface: A worker with goods has to shift them by hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' and 'to' only link; HANDLE means to deal in goods.
explanation.definitionFit: To manhandle something is to shift it by human strength alone, without machines.

clue.text: Club rotter left inside old vessel

parts.note: an iron is a golf club

indicators.note: inside puts the letter for left within the word for a rotter

parts.note: a cad is a rotter, a scoundrel

explanation.surface: A golfer's club and a scoundrel left aboard an ancient ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' puts the letter for left within the rotter, the club coming first.
explanation.definitionFit: An ironclad was a nineteenth-century warship protected by iron plates.

clue.text: A flighty female, the old king's representative?

definitions.meaning: the female of the ruff, a wading bird, so a female that flies
in medieval England an officer who managed a district for the crown or a lord

explanation.walkthrough: 'flighty' suggests a giddy woman, but it means simply that she flies: she is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The female ruff, a wader, has its own name, and the same word names a medieval local official; a sheriff was the shire's officer of this title.

clue.text: Somehow the Colonel's lot lost formation

indicators.note: somehow says the letters are rearranged in some unspecified way
lost tells us the letters of the word lot are taken away from the pool

parts.note: the words the and Colonel, the possessive adding no letter

explanation.surface: Somehow the colonel's troops broke ranks.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove L, O and T from THECOLONEL and rearrange the rest, HECONEL, as 'Somehow' and 'lost' direct.
explanation.definitionFit: An echelon is a stepped arrangement of troops, ships or aircraft, a military formation.

clue.text: Sound chap in Ohio, or one in ' Luzon, perhaps …

indicators.note: sound says the man's name is wanted for how it is pronounced, not its spelling

parts.note: Philip is a man's name, a chap
O was the old abbreviation for the US state of Ohio

explanation.surface: A man in Ohio is compared with someone from a Philippine island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' asks for the name as spoken, not spelt with PH. Luzon is the largest island of the Philippines. The dots run this clue on into 23-across.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Philippines, whose main island is Luzon, is a Filipino.

clue.text: Have reference to exercises unusual in art

parts.note: PE is physical education, school exercises

indicators.note: unusual says the letters of the two words in art appear in an odd order

explanation.surface: Gym sessions are rarely relevant to art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' scrambles the two words 'in art' after the exercises.
explanation.definitionFit: To pertain to something is to relate or belong to it.

clue.text: Around Los Angeles, a strange warning sound

indicators.note: around says the following pieces surround the city's abbreviation

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd or strange
LA is Los Angeles

explanation.surface: An odd alarm heard around LA.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' wraps the article and the slang word for odd about the city's abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Alarum is an old form of alarm, a call to arms or warning signal, as in Shakespeare's stage directions.

clue.text: . and not in Brunei, therefore

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the words that follow, Brunei and therefore

explanation.surface: A continuation: and it is not in Brunei either, therefore.
explanation.walkthrough: The run of letters spans 'Brunei, therefore'. The opening dots carry on from 20-across.
explanation.definitionFit: Neither, as in 'nor', is used to add a further negative, so it means also not.

clue.text: Part of 13 put underground

indicators.note: part of says only a portion of the referenced answer is used, its first five letters

parts.note: the answer to 13-across, the inland part of a country

explanation.surface: Part of something was buried.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the first five letters of the 13-across answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter is to bury a body in the ground.

clue.text: The road to Sandhurst — the Italian way of sending messages

parts.note: the A1 is Britain's Great North Road, its 1 written as the letter I
Sandhurst is the RMA, the Royal Military Academy where British army officers train
il is Italian for the

explanation.surface: Directions along the road to the officer academy, with an Italian touch for carrying letters.
explanation.walkthrough: The A1 is Britain's longest road, its 1 read as an I. 'to' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Letters sent by aeroplane rather than by land or sea go by this postal service.

clue.text: Does he back with this old coin?

definitions.meaning: a financial backer of a theatre production
an old English gold coin stamped with St Michael

explanation.walkthrough: 'back' means finance: a theatrical backer has this name. 'with' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a person who funds a stage show and a medieval English gold coin showing the archangel Michael.

clue.text: Anti-imperialist unimportant before Greenland riots

indicators.note: before puts the first word ahead of the rest in the answer

parts.note: little can mean trivial or of no importance

indicators.note: riots suggests disorder, so the letters of the island's name run wild

explanation.surface: An opponent of empire dismisses unrest in Greenland as trivial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'riots' scrambles the island's name, and 'before' puts the word for unimportant first.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase was used of Britons who opposed extending the Empire, wanting their country to keep to its own affairs.

clue.text: Reckless, politician abandoned sweetheart

indicators.note: abandoned means left behind, so the politician's letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: darling is an endearment for a sweetheart
L stands for a Liberal, a politician

explanation.surface: A careless politician has deserted their lover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reckless, politician' reads as a description of the politician, but 'Reckless' alone is the definition; removing L from DARLING leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A daring act is bold and heedless of danger.

clue.text: Apple for the dog?

definitions.meaning: the ... Orange is an old English apple variety
a breed of red-and-white toy spaniel

explanation.walkthrough: Both senses take their name from Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire. 'for the' only links the two.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs to an English dessert apple and to a variety of King Charles spaniel, both from the same Oxfordshire estate.
